description: Minion groups serve as a simple way to pit your characters against larger numbers of adversaries without bogging down combat encounters. These rules can also be used to represent groups of {@vehicle Interceptor Starfighter|starfighters|eoti} so that your player characters who want to play fighter aces can dogfight with multiple foes. The minion rules also let you represent several fighters flying in formation (usually a leader and one or two wingmates) for mutual defense and increased offensive power.

description.title: Applying Minion Rules to Fighters
entries: When using these rules, have all the pilots of a formation of two to four fighters be minions in the same minion group. These minions follow all the rules for minion groups found on page 132 of the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook. The important thing to note is that their ships also follow those rules.

A minion group of starfighters has a single {@rule hull trauma threshold} shared by all fighters in the group. The threshold is equal to the combined total of all of the fighters' {@rule hull trauma threshold|hull trauma thresholds}. The same applies to the group's combined {@rule system strain threshold}. Although standard minion groups do not have a strain threshold, minion groups of vehicles do have a {@rule system strain threshold}. Each time the group suffers hull trauma or system strain, you apply it to the group's threshold. Individual ships are destroyed or disabled each time the total hull trauma or system strain suffered exceeds a single starfighter's share of the group's threshold.

{@i You have a group of four minion pilots flying four Accipiter {@vehicle Interceptor Starfighter|interceptor starfighters|eoti}. The minion pilots each have a wound threshold of 4, so the group has a combined wound threshold of 16. The Accipiters have a {@rule hull trauma threshold} of 10 and {@rule system strain threshold} of 8, so the group has a combined {@rule hull trauma threshold} of 40 and {@rule system strain threshold} of 32.}

As with minion groups, characters do not attack a single starfighter, they attack the group as a whole. Narratively you may describe them as attacking an individual ship, but mechanically they're attacking the group.

Finally, just as {@rule Critical Injuries} instantly incapacitate a minion character, {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hits} immediately destroy a minion starfighter. This causes the group to immediately suffer hull trauma equal to the {@rule hull trauma threshold} of a single ship plus one. (This supersedes any other {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} results that would normally be rolled on {@table III.2-19: Vehicle Critical Hit Result} in the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook.)

{@i Gingrish Mrarrigh attacks the minion group from our previous example with the dual heavy beam cannon aboard his {@vehicle corvette||eoti}. He scores a hit and—through extraordinary rolling and a few useful talents—manages to deal 21 damage (after reduction from armor) and a {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} to the group. First the 21 damage eliminates two of the Accipiter fighters outright (since each one's hull threshold is only 10). Then the {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} causes the group to suffer an additional 11 hull trauma, which eliminates a third starfighter. The flight of Accipiters loses three of their number to one ferocious volley from Gingrish's ship!}

entries.title: Minion Groups Attacking and Making Skill Checks
entries: When a minion group of starfighters makes an attack (or another skill check like a {@skill Piloting} check), they make one check for the group. The dice pool is formed using the minion's characteristic, and their ranks in the skill equal to the number of minions in the group beyond the first. Also, remember minions can only have ranks in a skill that is listed as a group skill in their profile.

rule.name: Spending Advantage, Threat, Triumph, and Despair During Starship Combat
description: Although all the ways to spend dice pool results during combat found on page 104 of the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook are perfectly valid during starship combat, fighting in ships in space does have unique hazards and opportunities. We provide the suggestions in {@table 1-2: Spending Advantage and Triumph in Starship Combat} and {@table 1-3: Spending Threat and Despair in Starship Combat} as additional options for spending results. Hopefully they also give you inspiration for new and creative ways to interpret the dice pools at your own table.

_ref.name: Table 1-2: Spending Advantage and Triumph in Starship Combat
Table 1-3: Spending Threat and Despair in Starship Combat

rule.name: PCs as Starship Crew
description: Larger warships may have anywhere from a few dozen to a couple hundred crew members, with equal numbers of soldiers and passengers. So how does a group of three to six player characters control a large ship?

Generally when the player characters are in command of a starship, they should take on the role of the "bridge crew." They should be the heads of the various departments aboard a ship, the ones giving the orders to a larger cast of NPCs. This doesn't mean, however, that they don't get their hands dirty with piloting the ship, shooting the guns, and fixing whatever breaks. Instead, consider the PCs to be the most competent members of their departments, leading by example as they perform the tasks assigned to their departments. The goal is to make sure the PCs are the ones who are making most of the checks so that you, the GM, are not burdened with rolling a ton of NPC checks during each round.

The following section discusses these departments, the roles the PCs can adopt as the department heads, and the actions they may perform during a combat encounter. These roles are fairly generic, and the names may change depending on the faction that the ship is from or if the ship is even part of a formal navy.

_ref.name: Navigation Department and the Sailing Master
Gunnery Department and the Master Gunner
Engineering Department and the Chief Engineer
Medical Department and the Ship's Surgeon
Sensors and Communications and the Signals Officer

rule.name: Ship's Captain
description: Instead of being the head of a single department, the captain is in charge of the entire ship. While a good captain always listens to the advice of their subordinates, they are the ones who make the final decision.

Beyond making the decisions of where a ship goes, what it does, and who it fights, the captain can also directly oversee {@rule steering} the ship (especially if the PC who has taken on the role of captain has a high {@skill Operating} skill). In this case, the captain should make any {@skill Operating} checks and perform any {@b Pilot only} maneuvers and actions, but narratively they may have several NPCs helping them operate the controls.

It is also possible that the captain may be better suited to directing the fire of the ship's guns (especially if they have a high {@skill Gunnery} skill), so they could direct the fire of some of the ship's weapons while another PC or NPC handles piloting. Finally, some of the {@rule additional vehicle actions} found in {@table III.2-17: Additional Vehicle Actions} on page 229 of the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook may be appropriate for a captain, especially {@rule Fire Discipline} and {@rule Plot Course}.

rule.name: Navigation Department and the Sailing Master
description: The ship's navigation department, along with its head, the sailing master, is responsible for plotting courses and piloting the ship at both subluminal and superluminal speeds. This department is usually small even on large warships, with just three to six individuals.

The sailing master is the character who makes the {@skill Astrocartography|Astronavigation} checks to plot courses (especially when traveling at superluminal speeds). They can perform all of the {@b Pilot only} maneuvers and actions listed on pages 226-230 of the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook. They may also perform additional actions such as {@rule Plot Course}.

The extra members of the department help the sailing master manage all the controls and take watches when the sailing master is off duty. They do not confer any additional bonuses. However, if the ship has a particularly skilled crew, you may let them add {@dice boost} to the sailing master's checks or let one of them perform the {@rule Copilot} action in particularly dire circumstances.

rule.name: Gunnery Department and the Master Gunner
description: As you might expect, the gunnery department handles the ship's weapons. The master gunner (or the executive officer in some navies) is responsible for all the gun crews on their ship, as well as for assigning targets and directing fire. The size of the department depends on how many guns are on the ship. {@vehicle Dreadnought|Dreadnoughts|eoti} and {@vehicle Carrier|carriers|eoti} have similarly sized crew complements, but while a {@vehicle dreadnought||eoti} may have a third of its two hundred crew working guns, the {@vehicle carrier||eoti} might have a mere dozen crew in its gunnery department because of the relative lack of weapons.

The master gunner is the character who makes the {@skill Gunnery} checks to fire weapons and performs vehicle actions such as {@rule Blanket Barrage} and {@rule Concentrated Barrage}. They may also perform additional actions such as {@rule Intercept Projectiles}.

The gunnery department is often where the number of checks to be made can get out of hand, since warships may have scores of weapons. For this reason, we recommend the master gunner rely on the {@rule Concentrated Barrage} action when attacking enemy ships (or the {@rule Blanket Barrage} action when defending against a swarm of enemy {@vehicle Interceptor Starfighter|starfighters|eoti}).

The first combines the fire of multiple weapons of the same type (such as all the capital-grade beam turrets on a {@vehicle dreadnought||eoti}) into a single check that can do devastating damage. It can also be used to combine the fire from multiple antifighter weapons to target a single fighter or group of fighters.

The second lets you combine the fire of all your antifighter weapons in a single check to make it more difficult for fighters to attack your ship. If the master gunner is busy directing the fire of the ship's main weapons, this can be a good action for a PC with less {@skill Gunnery} skill or an NPC to perform.

rule.name: Engineering Department and the Chief Engineer
description: The engineering department oversees maintaining and repairing any mechanical and computer systems on the ship, although traditionally many engineers hold the reactors and main drives as their domain. The chief engineer oversees the department and personally signs off on any major repairs and modifications to the ship. On smaller vessels and civilian transports, the chief engineer may also be the only engineer aboard, while larger warships may have between twenty and fifty crew members as a part of engineering.

The chief engineer is the character who makes {@rule Damage Control} actions to repair hull trauma, system strain, and {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hits}. Although they may have several dozen crew members helping out, they are usually the only one to make the check. If a ship is large enough to have a sizable engineering department, then it's complicated enough that multiple people need to participate in any repair attempts. The chief engineer's check is as much about identifying problems and directing their underlings to fix the right things as it is making the repairs themselves.

The chief engineer may also perform some {@rule additional vehicle actions} (especially when their vehicle is still undamaged). Possibilities include {@rule Boost Defenses} to improve the ship's shielding and {@rule Hack Enemy's Systems} to bring down an enemy ship's vital operations (although they might fight for that chance with the ship's signals department). And if all else fails, the chief engineer might roll up their sleeves and fix problems with a sarween plasma welder and elbow grease, using the {@rule Manual Repairs} action.

rule.name: Medical Department and the Ship's Surgeon
description: The medical department is responsible for maintaining the health of the ship's crew. In peacetime, this is a mix of preventative medicine and treatment for accidental injuries. During a battle, however, the ship's surgeon and their orderlies try to save the lives of crew members injured during the fighting. On small ships, the ship's surgeon may be the only medical officer aboard, but on ships with several hundred crew or more, they usually have several orderlies or medics helping them in their duties.

At least one {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} can inflict wounds or {@rule Critical Injuries} on characters, as can {@symbols h} or {@symbols d} spent during combat. In addition, allied NPCs can be {@rule incapacitated} during combat and may die without treatment (see {@table 1-3: Spending Threat and Despair in Starship Combat}). The ship's surgeon makes the {@skill Medicine} checks to heal these characters.

rule.name: Sensors and Communications and the Signals Officer
description: The communications department and sensors department may be two separate departments or two branches of the same department under the command of the signals officer. Any warship of {@vehicle destroyer||eoti} size or larger usually has several crew members serving in these departments.

Most ships have some form of superluminal communication system, with a maximum effective range of a couple light years for coherent messages. They also carry subluminal backup systems with much shorter ranges, and a few ships even have message drones.

The types of sensors on a ship depend on the ship's role and the faction that fitted it out. Some vessels (especially scout ships and spy vessels) have powerful gravitic sensors that can detect superluminal ship movements from scores or even hundreds of light years away, but these are very rare, specialized, and ruinously expensive systems. A ship is much more likely to have a standard suite of passive sensors that can detect ships or other powered objects within the boundaries of a star system (strategic range) and a suite of active sensors that can be used to detect even unpowered objects or stealthed ships within long range (see page 137 of {@title Embers of the Imperium} for more information).

The signals officer can do plenty of things to aid their comrades during combat. They can interfere with enemy communications using the {@rule Jamming} action, analyze targets for weaknesses with {@rule Scan the Enemy}, defend against missiles and torpedoes with {@rule Intercept Projectiles}, and even access an enemy's computer systems and wreak havoc with {@rule Hack Enemy's Systems}. They may also attempt to intercept and decrypt enemy communications or pick up garbled messages from their allies.

rule.name: Mass Combat
description: Although the {@rule The Keleres of the Council|Keleres|eoti} generally conduct single-cohort missions and clandestine operations, as the galaxy descends into all-out war, they find themselves caught up in pitched battles more and more often. In rare cases, {@rule The Keleres of the Council|Keleres|eoti} may even lead larger forces, especially when those forces are arrayed against one of the Great Threats.

In the {@setting Twilight Imperium||eoti} setting, large-scale battles can act as excellent set pieces for climactic moments in a campaign and can provide characters who are not specialized in combat with a unique means of interacting with a fight. You can use them as a backdrop for a more personal conflict or have the PCs take a major part in the battles, even leading the forces involved.

The mass combat rules allow you to use the Narrative Dice System to abstractly represent the conflict and the PCs' roles within it. These rules facilitate interesting and unexpected outcomes without bogging gameplay down with too many details. You can also adjust them to fit battles of many different scales, from small engagements between squadrons of fighters or platoons of infantry to massive mech battles, {@vehicle dreadnought||eoti} engagements, or planetary invasions.

description.title: The Mass Combat Check
entries: To run a large-scale battle, you make a series of checks across the course of an encounter. These {@i mass combat checks} follow the rules for checks established in the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook. However, the number of dice and upgrades in the pool are determined by the details of the battle instead of the skills and characteristics of an individual character. The outcomes of these checks inform how the battle unfolds, from who is currently winning or losing to determining specific events on the battlefield.

At its core, a mass combat check represents the climax of a portion of a battle between an active force (usually the force the PCs are allied with) and the enemy force. As such, only one mass combat check is made per phase rather than one per side. Success on a mass combat check means that the active force has achieved their objective during that portion of the battle, while failure indicates temporary defeat.

_ref.name: Building a Mass Combat Check Dice Pool

rule.name: Phases
description: Before beginning a battle using the mass combat rules, divide the battle's timeline into a series of phases. These phases are conceptually the same as a round in a structured encounter: a period of time that gives everyone involved a chance to do something meaningful. The exact length of time each phase covers ranges from several minutes to several hours depending on the circumstances of the battle and the size of the forces involved.

When breaking down the battle into phases, make your divisions based on notable events that you plan on occurring during the battle. These events can be just about anything so long as they mark a potential point for the fight to shift in one side's favor or to move to a different arena. For example, a planetary invasion might use the following events: orbital bombardment, landing preliminary troops, and landing reinforcements.

description.title: Example Phases
entries: Although the phases in your battle depend on the specific events that occur, there are some phases that are general enough to be broadly useful. These are some examples:

items: {@b Deployment:} This phase covers moving forces into optimal positions for the coming battle, organizing supplies, and generally preparing for the upcoming fight. It usually has very little actual combat, but the preparations that take place can be crucial to determining the course of the battle.

{@b Opening Shots:} This is when the fighting starts. The two sides begin skirmishing with one another, testing each other's defenses and resolve. Sometimes one force may launch a lightning attack on the other to destabilize them or to gain some early advantage. This may not be the deciding moment of a battle, but it can set the tempo for the rest of the engagement.

{@b Main Engagement:} This is when the main fighting occurs. If the battle is particularly large, there may be several {@i main engagement} phases. Generally this is when the outcome of the battle is decided.

{@b Retreat, Pursue, Regroup:} This phase happens after the battle is finished, but it is still vitally important. If the PCs' forces defeated the opponent, they have the opportunity either to consolidate whatever gains they have earned or to pursue their foe to inflict further losses on them. Likewise, if the PCs were defeated, they have the chance to retreat in good order to preserve their forces rather than letting the foe wipe them out in a panicked rout.

description.title: Adjusting Phases as You Go
entries: Although you may plan on a specific set of phases for your battle, the dice results and your players' actions may change the course of events. In this case, you can change the future phases to fit the new circumstances or even add new phases to your battle.

However, when adding new phases or altering the course of your battle, you should always keep in mind the conditions for victory or defeat. You probably don't want your battle to keep dragging on without an end in sight! If you have a very complex battle in mind, it might make more sense to break it into several battles, each with their own victory conditions that help shape the events of the next battle.

description.title: Victory or Defeat
entries: When planning a mass combat battle, you should determine the conditions for victory for each side. Presumably, both sides have a reason for fighting the battle and you, as the GM, need to know what they are.

Generally, one side in a battle is the attacker, and the other is the defender. The attacker is trying to claim an objective or accomplish a goal, and the defender is trying to stop them. The objective could be to gain physical advantage. Examples include capturing fortifications, seizing supplies, or controlling some location of strategic value. It also could be attempting to destroy something: blowing up an ammunition depot, abducting or assassinating an enemy leader, or defacing a landmark that has great psychological importance to the enemy. Alternatively, the objective could be something intangible, such as simply demonstrating that the attacker can strike at will whenever and wherever they please.
In these situations, the defender's primary goal is to stop the attacker, with a secondary goal of hurting them enough to make the attacker think twice about trying it again in the future.

However, some battles (often referred to as {@i meeting engagements}) occur when two attacking forces crash into each other. The goals can be the same as previously mentioned for attackers, but in this case, {@i both} sides are trying to accomplish the same goal. The victor is the side that can accomplish it first.

rule.name: Building a Mass Combat Check Dice Pool
description: At the end of a given phase, the players construct and roll the mass combat dice pool assembled based on the events of that phase. To perform the one mass combat check for a phase, you first create a dice pool based on the current states of the active force and the enemy force, as well as any other battlefield conditions that apply.
Note that in all cases, {@b the active force is the force with the player characters}. Battles are always fought from the perspective of the group, whether they are attacking or defending.
To build the dice pool, use the following steps.

description.title: Step 1: Building the Ability of the Pool
entries: A mass combat dice pool is built using a very similar process to building the dice pool for a skill check. The main difference is instead of the number of Ability dice ({@dice ability}) and Proficiency dice ({@dice proficiency}) being determined by a single character's ranks in skills and characteristics, they are determined by the active force's ranks in {@b size} and {@b quality}.

Basically, the larger the force is, the higher its ranks in size are. Likewise, the better trained a force is, the higher its ranks in quality are. Obviously, this only takes into consideration the troops actively participating in the battle.

entries.title: Determining Ranks in Force Size
entries: Consult {@table 3-1: Force Size} for examples of forces of varying sizes and their corresponding ranks. The examples include infantry only, mechanized forces only, and units that combine both. If you have several very distinct and different units and you're not sure how their combined force fits into an example, look at each unit individually and figure out their individual ranks in size. Then determine the highest rank, and increase the overall rank of the acting force once to represent the reinforcing presence of the other smaller units. For example, if your acting force of starships consists of a {@b significant} force of three {@vehicle Interceptor Starfighter|interceptor|eoti} squadrons and an {@b imposing} flotilla of four {@vehicle Destroyer|destroyers|eoti} and one {@vehicle cruiser||eoti}, first you determine their ranks (2 and 3, respectively). Take the larger rank of 3, then increase it once to 4 to represent the presence of the {@vehicle Interceptor Starfighter|starfighters|eoti}. That determines your overall size rank of 4.

If your forces combine units of varying skill or equipment, don't worry, just add up the total sizes of the various units. The next section, {@b Determining Ranks in Force Quality}, describes how to combine units with different training or weapons and what effect that has on the mass combat dice pool.

entries.title: Determining Ranks in Force Quality
entries: Consult {@table 3-2: Force Quality} for examples of forces of varying quality and their corresponding ranks. Determine which examples most closely match the quality and equipment of the acting force, and that determines the acting force's ranks in quality.

If the active force consists of different units of varying abilities and equipment (such as a battalion of hundreds of conscripted militia with minimal training reinforced by a couple of ten-person squads of elite commandos), determine which unit is the largest (the unit with the most ranks in size), and determine that unit's ranks in quality. Then increase the ranks in quality for the acting force once to represent the presence of the more highly trained but smaller units. In our previous example, the {@b weak} force of unarmed militia would be combined with the {@b elite} force of commandos, increasing the quality of the overall force from {@b weak} to {@b untrained} (for 2 ranks in quality).

entries.title: Unusual Situations in Force Quality
entries: You may have situations where the training of the force does not match the quality of the equipment they are using. One example could be elite insurgents who have been fighting in their home territory for years but are armed with obsolete weapons and whatever they can salvage from the battlefield. Another could be corporate security forces who are given the very latest in weapons and armor but receive no real combat training. Which of these, training or equipment, that takes precedence is ultimately up to you, but we recommend you use the training and experience to set the force quality level rather than the equipment. Generally, skilled combatants know how to use old or outdated equipment effectively, while giving a neophyte a powerful weapon is just going to make them that much more overconfident and liable to do something foolish when the fighting starts.

entries.title: Applying Size and Quality to Build the Pool
entries: Once you have determined the size and quality of the acting force, you use the ranks in each to build the ability portion of the dice pool in the same manner you would a skill check. Select the larger of the two numbers. That is how many {@dice ability} you add to the pool. Then select the smaller of the two numbers. That is how many {@dice ability} in the pool that you upgrade into {@dice proficiency}.

description.title: Step 2: Building the Difficulty of the Pool
entries: Building the difficulty of the dice pool (i.e. determining how many Difficulty [{@dice difficulty}] and Challenge [{@dice challenge}] dice are in the pool) follows the same steps as building the ability of the dice pool.

First, determine the ranks in size and quality of the enemy force using the same metrics as explained in {@b Step 1}. Once you have determined the size and quality of enemy force, select the larger of the two ranks. This is how many {@dice difficulty} you add to the pool. Then select the smaller of the two ranks. This is how many {@dice difficulty} in the pool that you upgrade into {@dice challenge}.

description.title: Step 3: Boost and Setback Dice
entries: Once you have determined the ability and difficulty of the dice pool based on the size and quality of the two forces, you have the chance to add Boost dice {@dice boost} and Setback dice {@dice setback} based on other elements that may affect the battle. These can include the morale of the forces, circumstances on the battlefield, actions taken by the PCs, and anything else you or your group can come up with. Elements that benefit the active force add {@dice boost} to the pool, while elements that benefit the enemy add {@dice setback} to the pool. {@table 3-3: Boost and Setback in Mass Combat} on page 29 offers a list of suggested reasons for adding {@dice boost} and {@dice setback} to the mass combat check. These are just a jumping-off point to help you and your players generate ideas about the kinds of things that may affect the check.

_ref.name: Story Points and Talents in Mass Combat Checks
Table 3-3: Boost and Setback in Mass Combat

description.title: Step 4: Upgrading and Downgrading the Check
entries: Most of the time, once you have determined the ability and difficulty of the mass combat check, you do not upgrade or downgrade the check further. However, in some circumstances abilities, talents, or the results of previous mass combat checks may cause the check to be upgraded or downgraded. Apply those upgrades and downgrades during this step by following the rules on page 22 of the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook, with upgrades being applied before downgrades.

description.title: Step 5: Removing Dice
entries: If any rules, talents, abilities, or circumstances instruct you to remove dice from the dice pool, do so during this step by following the rules on page 23 of the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook.

description.title: Step 6: Resolving the Check Results
entries: Now that the dice pool has been constructed, it's time to roll the dice and see what happens! The results of the check determine the success or failure of the active force during that phase and may well have repercussions on later phases of the combat.

On a successful check, the active force accomplishes its objectives for that phase of the battle or prevents the enemy force from achieving its goals. Those goals should have been determined per {@b Victory or Defeat} on page 25. Additional {@symbols s} can be spent to achieve further goals or to increase the magnitude of the success.

In some cases, the degree of success may be defined by how many {@symbols s} your players spend. For example, if the objective of the battle was to hold out long enough to evacuate a town or to attempt to destroy a bunch of enemy infrastructure, each {@symbols s} may represent a percentage of civilians evacuated or infrastructure destroyed.
If the active force fails the check, the enemy force accomplishes its objectives for that phase of the battle or the active force is stymied.

{@symbols a}, {@symbols t}, {@symbols h}, and {@symbols d} can be spent narratively from this check or by using the suggestions found in {@table 3-4: Spending Advantage and Triumph in Mass Combat} or {@table 3-5: Spending Threat and Despair in Mass Combat} on page 32.

_ref.name: Table 3-4: Spending Advantage and Triumph in Mass Combat
Table 3-5: Spending Threat and Despair in Mass Combat

rule.name: Where the PCs Fit In
description: Where do the PCs fit into all this? PCs are, by their very nature, wild cards. As the heroes of the narrative, they fill many vital roles on the field of mass combat. With a few exceptions, the PCs are likely some of the most qualified and skilled individuals in the active force. While they can't win a battle on their own, they can have a significant effect on the outcome.

The following are some of the ways the PCs participate in a mass combat. Each of these options takes up the majority of a PC's time during a given phase, meaning the PC can't be doing this and something else at the same time.

Note, the checks the PCs make in this section are standard skill checks, not mass combat checks. When spending {@symbols a}, {@symbols h}, {@symbols t}, and {@symbols d}, do {@b not} use {@table 3-4: Spending Advantage and Triumph in Mass Combat|Table 3-4} and {@table 3-5: Spending Threat and Despair in Mass Combat|Table 3-5} (unless, as the GM, you think a result is highly appropriate to the situation). Instead, use the tables for spending these results found on pages 104 and 121 of the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook, or perhaps you and your players can come up with something that fits the ongoing narrative!

description.title: Leading the Fight
entries: If a PC is particularly skilled at {@skill Leadership} or has some rank or authority with the active force (or both), they can easily be the person commanding the active force. If a PC is in command, they can use their knowledge of leadership and tactics to direct that phase of the battle.

To do so, the PC should make a {@difficulty daunting|leadership}. If they succeed, their inspired tactics and charisma push the active force to even greater heights. During the next phase of the battle, the active force may count their ranks in quality as equal to the PC's ranks in the {@skill Leadership} skill, instead of their normal quality.

If the active force's quality is already equal to the PC's ranks in {@skill Leadership}, the active force increases its ranks in quality by 1 instead, to a maximum of 6 (this specifically increases ranks over the normal limit of 5, and represents the effect great leadership can have on even very skilled troops).

description.title: Supporting the Troops
entries: Many PCs have skills that they can use to support the active force. The possibilities are only limited by your approval as GM and your players' imaginations, but here are some suggestions. Each is an activity designed to be performed by one or two PCs during a single phase and includes a suggested skill check the PC can make. You can adjust the default difficulties based on the ongoing narrative. A desperate battle in a hostile environment or against a powerful enemy force may result in the difficulty being increased by 1 or 2 for many or all of these checks.

items: {@b Scouting the battlefield:} The PC can scout out enemy positions, deployments, and intervening terrain or weather by making an {@difficulty average|survival}. If this is a space battle, they can make an {@difficulty average|astrocartography} instead.
{@b Repairing damaged vehicles or ships:} The PC can help fix and direct the repairs of damaged ships and vehicles with an {@difficulty average|mechanics}.
{@b Battlefield medicine:} The PC can care for wounded soldiers and sailors, keeping the numbers of dead low and improving the morale of their comrades with an {@difficulty average|medicine}.
{@b Coordinate fire support:} The PC can guide attacks from artillery or other long range weapons to improve their accuracy and effectiveness with an {@difficulty easy|knowledge (science)||eoti}.

{@b Hack enemy systems and protect friendly networks:} The PC can either hack into enemy computer and communication networks to sow chaos and disruption or protect their own side's networks from the same fate with an {@difficulty average|computers}.

{@b Leading from the front:} The PC can lead elements of the active force from the front lines by making an {@difficulty easy|leadership}. If they succeed, they inspire the soldiers around them by showing that the PC is willing to brave danger alongside them.
{@b Know your enemy:} The PC can study the enemy to see if they are predisposed to certain tactics or cultural blind spots with an {@difficulty easy|knowledge (culture)||eoti}.

entries: If the PC performs this action successfully, they either add {@dice boost} to the mass combat check made at the end of the current phase or they remove {@dice setback} from that check, depending on their actions and the ongoing narrative. If they're doing something specifically to enhance their own forces, they should probably add {@dice boost}. On the other hand, if they're doing something to counteract a problem or an enemy effort that is already adding {@dice setback} to the next check, they should probably remove that {@dice setback} instead.

However, if the PCs generate at least {@symbols sss} on their check, they can choose to add {@symbols s} to the results of the mass combat check rather than adding {@dice boost} or removing {@dice setback}. Their impressive efforts have guaranteed they have affected the results.

description.title: Getting Involved Directly
entries: Combat-focused PCs can also get directly involved in the fighting. When they do this, they take up a position on the front lines, perhaps piloting a {@vehicle Interceptor Starfighter|starfighter|eoti}, manning the guns on a starship, firing heavy weapons in a forward strongpoint, or driving a mech. This can be a more appealing option for combat-focused PCs. However, it's also more difficult for a single person to make a difference in the swirling melee of combat, and there is the very real risk of suffering an injury in the process.

To get involved directly, the PC makes a {@difficulty hard} combat check using their preferred combat skill that also makes the most sense given the battle (if the battle is in space, for example, the PC probably shouldn't use the {@skill Brawl} or {@skill Melee} skill). If they succeed, they add {@dice boost} to the next mass combat check made at the end of the current phase. If they fail, they suffer 4 wounds, plus 1 additional wound for each {@symbols h} generated on the check.

If the PC generates at least {@symbols sss} on their check, they can also choose to inflict one {@rule Critical Injuries|Critical Injury} on a notable adversary involved in the battle, or one {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} on an enemy vehicle involved in the battle (this is in addition to the {@dice boost} they add to the check). They may have either caused the injury themselves, or put the adversary in a dangerous situation because of their actions.

description.title: Crisis Points
entries: Crisis points are the final option and the most cinematic. They represent circumstances where a small group of people can turn the tide of battle with their daring and cunning actions. They can either be a moment of opportunity for the active force or a grave danger that must be dealt with. In either case, they are circumstances outside of the larger battle that the PCs must deal with as a group.
Some examples of crisis points include the following:

items: A chance encounter on the battlefield reveals the location and relative vulnerability of the enemy commander. If the PCs act quickly, they can attack the commander directly and decapitate the enemy force's leadership.
The enemy force's top fighter ace is leading an enemy fighter assault. If the PCs engage and destroy them in front of their entire fighter corps, the enemy fighters lose morale and flee.
A gap in the defenses of an enemy fortification allows the PCs to slip inside and destroy the main power generators, shutting down the defense grids protecting the enemy's planetary defense systems.
The PCs have access to a ship capable of boarding the enemy's chief command and control vessel. If they can take over that vessel, the enemy fleet may collapse into disarray.
An enemy infiltration team suddenly attacks the active force's headquarters, forcing the PCs into a ferocious fight to keep their own leadership alive.

Sabotage cripples a powerful warship of the active force, leaving it drifting out of control. If the PCs don't defend it from an oncoming bomber wave, the ship is destroyed, and as a result, the fleet is lost.

Under the command of a subordinate, some of the active force turns traitor. If the PCs don't deal with the subordinate and their most powerful warriors, the active force has an additional enemy army in its midst.

entries: All of these can be run as a structured encounter (or set of encounters, depending on their complexity). They take the place of whatever else the PCs were planning to do during that phase.

entries.title: Using and Resolving Crisis Points
entries: Crisis points are disruptive enough that you shouldn't employ them in every mass combat. In fact, they're usually only the result of a mass combat check generating {@symbols tt} or {@symbols dd} (see {@table 3-4: Spending Advantage and Triumph in Mass Combat} and {@table 3-5: Spending Threat and Despair in Mass Combat}).

The results of the crisis point depend on whether it was added due to {@symbols t} or {@symbols d}. The former are opportunities to either win the battle outright or gain such a significant advantage on the next mass combat check that the active force is very likely to win. The latter are emergencies that cause the active force to lose the battle outright unless the PCs successfully intervene. Even if they do succeed, however, the mass combat continues.

Of course, as the GM, you are allowed to add a crisis point to a mass combat even without spending {@symbols t} or {@symbols d}. This can either be an opportunity for the PCs or an emergency for them to deal with. However, since the crisis point can often end the battle, we recommend adding a crisis point only for particularly climactic and cinematic events in your campaign. In short, crisis points have the potential to be very exciting and memorable events, so use them sparingly to keep them from becoming mundane.

rule.name: Tallying the Cost of Battle
description: In a battle, soldiers are killed and wounded and ships or vehicles are destroyed or damaged. For the most part, these consequences are handled narratively when using the mass combat rules. However, we do provide some guidelines for how to determine casualties based on the results of the battle.

description.title: Basic Casualties
entries: Although it is possible to fight a battle without casualties, it's unlikely. At the end of the mass combat, you can determine basic casualties suffered by the active and the enemy force using the following guidelines:

items: The losing side in the mass combat always suffers enough casualties to decrease its ranks in size by 1.

The losing side in the mass combat also suffers enough casualties to decrease its ranks in size by 1 again, {@i unless} the losing side performed particularly well despite having lost. Mechanically, this could have been failing the last couple mass combat checks with {@symbols aaa} or {@symbols t}. Narratively, this could be based on the actions that key characters on that side took during the combat.

The winning side in the mass combat suffers enough casualties to decrease its ranks in size by 1, {@i unless} the winning side performed particularly well in addition to winning. Mechanically, this could have been succeeding the last couple mass combat checks with {@symbols aaa} or {@symbols t}. Narratively, this could be based on the actions that key characters on that side took during the combat.

entries.title: Additional Casualties
entries: The size of the acting and enemy force can also be reduced during the combat by some of the results from {@table 3-4: Spending Advantage and Triumph in Mass Combat|Table 3-4} and {@table 3-5: Spending Threat and Despair in Mass Combat|Table 3-5}. These reductions also apply at the end of the combat, after basic casualties have been applied.

In addition, some actions that characters take or some of the other results during the combat can cause individual vehicles and starships to be damaged or destroyed. It is up to you as the GM to determine whether these losses are enough to affect the overall size rank of the force they belonged to (although the ship or vehicle is still damaged or destroyed, whether it affects the size or not).

description.title: Interpreting Casualties
entries: When the size of forces are reduced, the numbers that make up that force are reduced. Consult {@table 3-1: Force Size|Table 3-1} to see how many soldiers, vehicles, or starships the new size rank represents. Simply put, the difference in numbers between the start and the end of the battle is the number of casualties that force suffers.

This doesn't mean, however, that all those soldiers are dead, or all those vehicles are destroyed. In military terms, casualties can refer to dead, wounded, or missing soldiers, and we use the term in the same way here. Out of the total casualties suffered, a minority of those lost are actually killed, while the rest are either injured, have been captured by the enemy, or ended up fleeing the battlefield and will return later. The same holds true for vehicles and starships. Many of those lost are not completely destroyed, but instead were damaged to the point that they couldn't fight, were abandoned by their crews, or had to flee the battlefield.

What percentage of casualties are dead or destroyed versus injured or damaged is up to you as the GM, and can be determined based on the events of the battle. However, if you need rough guidelines, you can assume casualties are divided into thirds, with a third of the casualties being dead, a third injured, and a third fled or captured (or their vehicular equivalent).

entries.title: Reduced to 0 Ranks
entries: If a force is reduced to 0 ranks in size, then it has been completely wiped out. Again, not everyone is dead, but those who were not slain have fled in a panicked rout, been captured as prisoners, or are injured (or some combination thereof). It's up to you whether they have any chance of regrouping into any sort of fighting force in the future.

entries.title: Recovering
entries: Recovering from casualties is an entirely narrative exercise and somewhat beyond the mass combat rules. Just remember that all sorts of factors can affect how long it takes to rebuild a fighting force. Available reinforcements, efforts to rally and regroup soldiers who fled the battlefield, and treating the wounded after the fight may all affect how quickly a unit can reconstitute its strength.

vehicle.name: Perspeculor Survey Vehicle

abilities.name: All-Terrain
abilities.description: When making a {@skill Driving} check to direct the vehicle, your character may remove {@dice setback|2} added to the check due to terrain.

description: Even with a galaxy-spanning empire, there are still countless worlds yet to be explored. For centuries, Vectura Rex has supplied those efforts with the hardy Perspeculor. Built to withstand harsh environments, it can be pressurized, seal itself against {@rule vacuum} or poisonous atmospheres, and even operate submerged in a limited capacity. Four large all-weather wheels on a reinforced suspension system carry a durable rectangular crew and cargo cabin. The Perspeculor can carry up to ten passengers and crew, plus their gear, for limited runs. For extended expeditions, it is more comfortably crewed by a maximum of six to allow room for supplies and living space. Most of the seats transform into single beds, while more beds fold down from the walls or roof.

The vehicle can be outfitted with an array of accessories depending on the intended mission. Remote control lights, cameras, sensors, manipulator arms, drone docking stations, sample storage containers, winches, and even small {@vehicle Personal Transport (Monoride)|monorides|eoti} can be fitted to the exterior.

The interior is typically divided into a living space and a workspace. Lab stations, workstations, sensors, tools, computers, and gear storage make up the workspace. The living space contains most of the converted beds, a tiny galley, and the other necessary facilities for self-sufficient exploration. The passenger side hatch is even a single-person airlock.

vehicle.name: Predator Rambler

weapons.name: 1 turret-mounted light mass driver
weapons.details: May not be used against targets within short range.

description: Given Aether Cosmos's attempts to resist {@rule Federation of Sol|Sol's|eoti} expansion toward their world, it's an ironic quirk of galactic economics that they once supplied the {@rule Federation of Sol|Federation|eoti} with a rugged and reliable infantry fighting vehicle.

The Predator eschews fancy hover-tech or articulated legs in favor of six oversized tires and a tough suspension. The enclosed and armored cab has enough room for a squad of soldiers along with their gear. Most importantly, the remote-controlled turret on the Predator's roof is large enough to mount a small but potent mass driver and coaxial blazer for anti-infantry work.

Eventually, {@rule Federation of Sol|Federation|eoti} procurement decided to shift away from foreign suppliers, and their forces began phasing out the Predators. At that point, they did what the {@rule Federation of Sol|Federation|eoti} so often does and dumped them en masse into the secondary market, ensuring mercenaries, private security forces, and independent worlds across the galaxy would have a cheap supply of light military vehicles for decades to come. A dozen of these ended up being donated to the {@rule The Keleres of the Council|Keleres|eoti} and were received enthusiastically by the Custodian quartermasters. Although they are becoming temperamental with age, they are still highly valued by any {@rule The Keleres of the Council|Keleres|eoti} with a militaristic bent.

vehicle.name: Valiant Emergency Response Vehicle
vehicle.complement: 1 driver, 1 leader, and 4 emergency techs and/or security officers
vehicle.encumbranceCapacity: 5, plus personal firefighting equipment and rescue tools for all passengers and 1 inflatable boat

abilities.name: All-Terrain
abilities.description: When making a {@skill Driving} check to direct the vehicle, your character may remove {@dice setback|2} added to the check due to terrain.

description: Aether Cosmos's Valiant emergency response vehicles are all-in-one fast response units ready to meet a variety of everyday crises. The Valiant's crew can fight fires, provide medical care, conduct rescues, and perform light security. The vehicle's boxy but efficient cabin rides on six large wheels suited for use on or off the road. A four-person cab opens into a secondary compartment that holds four additional fold-down seats and gear storage. The rear compartment carries two grav-stretchers stored in the floor and medical supplies within locked wall cabinets. The compartment can also be refitted to transport restrained detainees. The Valiant has two side doors and a rear hatch that folds down and extends to create a steep ramp.

Firefighting equipment, hoses, an inflatable rescue boat, and additional gear are stored on the vehicle's roof, attached to outer panels or beneath the rear compartment. The Valiant's powerful engine sits under the cab and secondary compartment and can be accessed through the latter's floor. The bottom of the vehicle is protected by stout metal belly panels. The Valiant is lightly armored to resist minor attacks or hazardous conditions, but it is not military grade. It is fitted with a top-mounted water cannon that is intended for firefighting, though it can also be used for crowd control.

vehicle.name: Centipede Segmented Mech

abilities.name: All-Terrain
abilities.description: When making a {@skill Driving} check to direct the vehicle, your character may remove {@dice setback|2} added to the check due to terrain.

abilities.name: Centipede Chain
abilities.description: Centipede mechs have cargo units linked to the operation unit. Cargo units cost 5,000 aurei. Each cargo unit added to the chain increases the hull trauma and system strain thresholds of the combined unit by 10 and increases the encumbrance capacity by 100. For every three cargo units, increase the silhouette of the entire vehicle by 1.

description: Mechs are largely known for their military applications, but some civilian uses exist, especially where terrain is rough in undeveloped or underdeveloped locales. Aether Cosmos's Centipede line of mechs are rugged transport vehicles that share some design concepts with the Cavalcade bulk haulers. The mechs aren't fast, but they can carry goods across rough terrain at a height that towers over smaller vehicles and obstacles.

Aether Cosmos offers industry-specific customizations, but at their core, Centipede mechs combine into a chain of hauler units, each with their own propulsion drives and large cargo containers. Each mech has four stout, tough legs extending from the sides. At the front is the operation unit, with a slightly elevated cab for better visibility. Although the crew can hop from one hauler to the next, only a brave or foolish individual would do so while the Centipede is underway.

vehicle.name: Crystal Carriage

abilities.name: Vulnerable
abilities.description: All successful combat checks targeting this vehicle add {@symbols aa} to the results.

description: Few vehicles scream wealth and attention like Prismetra's double-decker Crystal Carriage. Clad entirely in reinforced transparent panels, the vehicle appears as though it was sculpted out of an enormous chunk of high-quality cut and polished crystal, riding on a platform of burnished copper and gold. Of course, individual panels can be changed from fully transparent to fully reflective or anywhere in between, depending on whether the riders wish to be seen by the public.

As a hovering grav-field vehicle, the carriage's underside contains the necessary equipment concealed by more reflective panels. The vehicle is as long and tall as a typical high-capacity bus. The upper level is about two thirds the length of the lower level and centered lengthwise. It is split into two compartments that serve as the primary riding and entertainment areas. A spiral staircase leads to the lower level. The front half of that level is dedicated to the driver's cab, crew seats, food and drink preparation stations, and other equipment necessary to serve the riders. The back half typically contains a compact but opulent living and sleeping space.

vehicle.name: Hercules Multiconstruction Vehicle

abilities.name: Bulldozer
abilities.description: When the Hercules deliberately {@rule Collisions|collides} with another vehicle (see page 222 of the {@title Genesys} Core Rulebook), the Hercules reduces the results of the {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} it suffers by 20. The other vehicle suffers 8 damage to its hull trauma threshold and increases the results of the {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} it suffers by 40.

abilities.name: Manipulator Arm/Crane
abilities.description: While operating the manipulator arm/crane, your character may make a {@difficulty hard|operating} to pick up and move a stationary object within short range that is silhouette 2 or smaller.

description: The Hercules Multiconstruction vehicle is Aether Cosmos's most successful heavy machinery multi-tool. The core of the vehicle is an enormous single all-terrain sphere. The surface of the sphere has a multiphase, adaptable traction coating which the driver can adjust to match the terrain. It can change from road treads to rugged knobs for off-road use. This feature makes the vehicle highly maneuverable and able to roll in any direction at any time. Above the sphere is the engine and control cab, affording an unobstructed view in all directions. This large vehicle can still technically drive on public roads, though it dominates the lanes. Additionally, light roads, standard road surfaces, and bridges may not have the strength to support the focused weight of the sphere.

Mounted around the sphere at equidistant points are three common construction apparatuses. Each can be lifted or retracted while not in use. One is a large bulldozer blade, such as has been used for centuries. Another is a large telescoping manipulator arm that can also be aligned in a straight configuration for use as a crane. When the arm is used, outriggers are deployed to keep the unit stable. Finally, the Hercules has a large fusion plate similar in size to the bulldozer blade. When the plate folds down, it heats or fuses whatever material it contacts — natural or synthetic — into solid slabs. The Hercules rolls alongside the future road or area to be fused, keeping the heavy sphere out of the construction path while leveling it. Companies can purchase the vehicle with other attachments, but they are not easily swapped out after manufacture due to strict balancing requirements. Some additions make the Hercules too big to travel on public roads without additional transport and special provisions. Custom equipment is most common for units that serve a single industrial location.

vehicle.name: Buzzer Repair Pod
description: Aether Cosmos's Buzzer repair pods are vehicles in name only; a single-pilot cockpit strapped to an engine assembly and bristling with claws, cutters, welders, and other tools inside the craft. Some tools are on dedicated rigs, but most are used via a pair of flexible manipulator arms at the front of the pod.

Small thrusters provide 360-degree movement. Accessible by a single rear hatch, the pod is pressurized for use without environment suits, but large enough to accommodate them should the workers need to exit for any reason. The pods only function in {@rule gravity|zero gravity}; they are unable to fly or maneuver in atmosphere or significant {@rule gravity}.

The Buzzer can move equipment and large pieces of structure. It often takes more than one pod to place items much larger than themselves, though. Multi-pod efforts ensure better handling and more accurate guiding. For this reason, many dockyards keep a mini fleet of Buzzers on hand.

vehicle.name: Serpens Investigator

abilities.name: Mk4 Salaagh Survey Sensor Pack
abilities.description: When making a {@skill Perception} check using the ship's sensors, your character may add {@symbols s} to the results.

abilities.name: Antagonistic Sensor Baffle
abilities.description: Checks made to detect or spot this ship add {@symbols fh} to the results. Characters aboard this ship may choose to spend {@symbols h} from those checks to inflict 2 system strain per {@symbols h} spent on the vehicle where the check originated. If they do so, this ship suffers 2 system strain.

weapons.name: Javis interceptor dart launcher
weapons.details: If an attack with this weapon misses, the {@quality Guided} quality triggers without spending {@symbols aa}.

description: The Serpens Investigator has the dubious distinction of being one of the few starships to be subjected to an "anti-marketing" campaign by its manufacturer. In fact, Vectura Rex categorically denies producing the compact, long-range, and heavily armed vessel at all. After all, any construction of such a potent vessel would violate all sorts of laws governing civilian ships. So, Vectura Rex has not been constructing a small but steady supply of Serpens (in various models) for the Winnarian Custodian Guard for the past several centuries. And it {@i certainly} has not produced as many as four Serpens for the {@rule The Keleres of the Council|Keleres|eoti} after their founding, on specific request of the Custodians who liaise with the organization.

One look at the Serpens and it's easy to understand why the ships are as prized as they are illegal. Each ship is no larger than a {@vehicle star bomber||eoti}, but their nondescript outer hulls are packed to the bulkheads with sensors, stealth systems, and state-of-the-art weapons quietly obtained from manufacturers across several of the Great Civilizations. That they carry all this plus a dozen passengers and crew and still manage a decent superluminal range is a fantastically expensive marvel of engineering.

vehicle.name: Merchant Master Cargo Ship
vehicle.complement: 1 pilot, 1 copilot, 1 cargo master, 2 crew, 5 guards
description: Prismetra's Merchant Master cargo ship is the company's most important offering for the lucrative freight market. {@rule Emirates of Hacan|Hacan|eoti} traders drove much of Prismetra's early success thanks to this and similar cargo ships. The Merchant Master is a premium craft far above the utilitarian cargo ships most companies sell. It is ornate and highly customized to the buyer's needs. This flair doesn't come cheap, but purchasers of the Merchant Master know that the look of the ship is an important part of selling their goods anywhere in the galaxy. No two Merchant Masters ever appear completely the same, but they operate very similarly.

For the exterior, form definitely wins over function. All circuits, conduits, and machinery are concealed behind hull plating, louvers, screens, and retractable panels. Every color and finish on the exterior can be customized. Nestled among the lighted trim are long video panels that can display the ship's information in flight, but they mainly serve as advertisements when operating in busy ports.

vehicle.name: Interstellar Messenger Courier Ship
vehicle.encumbranceCapacity: 15 (40 without passengers)
description: {@vehicle Courier Ship|Courier ships|eoti} are vital to interstellar communications across the galaxy, thanks to the limited range of FTL transmissions. Prismetra's Interstellar Messenger is similar to other {@vehicle Courier Ship|courier ships|eoti} in that it is very fast and lightweight, with an impressive array of broadcast communication devices. It is better armored than average and mounts a light turret for self-defense. These features come at the expense of cargo capacity, shields, and superluminal range. The ship also requires an extra crew member dedicated to managing the communications array and gun.

Prismetra's model is very popular with its {@rule Emirates of Hacan|Hacan|eoti} government and commercial customers. {@rule Emirates of Hacan|Hacan|eoti} officials looking to conduct business while also being prepared for conflict are quite willing to tolerate a ship that must make more frequent supply stops in exchange for extra defensive capabilities. The extra crew makes communications transfers more efficient and provides redundancy should anyone become injured or incapacitated.

The Interstellar Messenger can hold up to three passengers in its cramped confines. The {@rule Emirates of Hacan|Hacan|eoti} government regularly makes use of this feature to transport diplomats and corporate negotiators to hot spots. This is useful when their swift physical presence is more important than the show of formality conferred by an {@vehicle overture cutter||eoti}.

vehicle.name: Quest Scientific Research Vessel
vehicle.encumbranceCapacity: 150, plus 2 {@vehicle Shuttle|shuttles|eoti}

abilities.name: Laboratory
abilities.description: While in the laboratory, your character adds {@dice boost|2} to any {@skill Astrocartography}, {@skill Computers}, {@skill Knowledge}, {@skill Mechanics}, and {@skill Medicine} skill checks they make. Any {@symbols a} can be cumulatively spent to reduce any time requirements by 25%, up to 75%.

weapons.name: 1 port and 1 starboard dual short-barreled autocannon

description: Self-contained laboratories prepared to operate far from civilization, Prismetra's Quest ships are normally sponsored by governments, factions, educational institutions, or corporations. A few freelance vessels exist, sometimes supporting independent explorers and scouts, but they often have ulterior motives and poor ethics.

Quest vessels have an atypical vertical layout, with floors arranged more like an office building than the horizontal plans of many starships. This reduces the Quest's landing footprint, allowing for a wider variety of possible landing sites in rugged terrain. Each of the levels has one to four rooms. The lower levels contain labs and equipment. The middle levels feature common work and living areas. The upper levels hold the crew quarters. The top level holds the main command center floor.

The exact equipment carried aboard the Quest depends on the mission. All models are capable of surveying star systems and planets, keeping watch on the surroundings when landed, and performing basic scientific studies. Specialized equipment can be swapped as needed, although installation and calibration take time. The Quest provides good protection for its crew. Though light on armor, its shields are better than average for vehicles of its type. It also carries light weapons for fending off pirates or other hostiles, and internal magen fields in case an "experimental sample" breaks out of containment.

vehicle.name: Breaker Salvage Ship
vehicle.encumbranceCapacity: 500, plus 5 repair pods and 2 {@vehicle Shuttle|shuttles|eoti}

abilities.name: Extra Plating
abilities.description: When this ship is fully loaded with salvaged plating, increase the armor value by 1.

weapons.name: 1 port, 1 starboard, and 2 ventral short-barreled autocannon turrets

description: After millennia of war and interstellar travel, derelict ships litter the galaxy. Whether floating adrift and forgotten in space or crumpled half-buried on an inhospitable world, these ships often still have value to those willing to seek them out. Most of the possible wealth comes in the form of scrap metal, rare alloys, and reusable parts. Occasionally, old technology, lost treasures, and other oddities make things more interesting or increase profitability.

Aether Cosmos's Breaker salvage ships are ill-proportioned and blocky, mostly just enormous holds designed to store machinery and massive salvaged items. Arm-mounted plasma cutters shear hull plating straight off a wreck while mag-grapples hold the panels and then maneuver them to exterior racks along the sides of the Breaker. These stacks of salvaged plating effectively add armor to the Breaker.

Salvage crews work from repair pods and in reinforced spacesuits. Aboard the Breaker, techs evaluate usable equipment and junk the rest. Salvage ships can stay out for months at a time, picking a system clean before returning to a port with their haul.

vehicle.name: Rampart Vault Ship
vehicle.encumbranceCapacity: 600, plus 3 {@vehicle Shuttle|shuttles|eoti}

abilities.name: Resilient
abilities.description: When this vehicle suffers a {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} while your character is operating it, you may spend a Story Point to roll a second result and choose the result you prefer.

weapons.name: 3 forward and 3 aft heavy beam cannon turrets
weapons.fireArc: Forward, Port, and Starboard or Aft, Port, and Starboard

weapons.name: 1 dorsal, 1 ventral, 1 port, and 1 starboard antifighter beam turret
weapons.details: When attacking a target of silhouette 4 or smaller, reduce difficulty by 1.

description: Few targets light up a pirate's eyes like Vectura Rex's Rampart vault ships. Legends surrounding long lost treasure ships of the Lazax Empire continue to fuel expeditions to recover ancient wealth and untold riches, but vault ships still fly today, hauling valuable goods from one side of the galaxy to the other.

Vectura Rex's current offering is an incrementally updated version of their tried-and-true ancient design. The Rampart vault ship was designed around durability, defense, and escape. For durability and defense, it uses nano-welded duranium hull plating, reinforced with powerful magen screens and significant defensive weaponry.

For escape, the Rampart has a trick called the escape triad. When implemented, the Rampart divides itself into separate vessels, splitting the ship in thirds. Normally, these thirds provide redundancy for the complete ship. One ship's command center can take over for another, for example. The escape triad can also turn undamaged portions of the ship into lifeboats, should the Rampart take significant damage.

The vaults of the ship are protected by layers of composite armor. Unless access is required during the voyage, the vaults are fully sealed with the doors welded closed and interiors filled with inert but nonbreathable gases. Automated defenses, backed up by soldiers, protect the corridors around the vault. There are true tales of vaults surviving the destruction of a Rampart and later being found buried in a crash site or floating among space debris.

vehicle.name: Rampart Vault Ship (Escape Triad)
vehicle.encumbranceCapacity: 200, plus 1 {@vehicle Shuttle|shuttle|eoti}

abilities.name: Resilient
abilities.description: When this vehicle suffers a {@rule Vehicle Critical Hits|Critical Hit} while your character is operating it, you may spend a Story Point to roll a second result and choose the result you prefer.

weapons.name: 1 forward and 1 aft heavy beam cannon turrets
weapons.fireArc: Forward, Port, and Starboard or Aft, Port, and Starboard

weapons.name: 1 dorsal, 1 port, and 1 starboard antifighter beam turret
weapons.details: When attacking a target of silhouette 4 or smaller, reduce difficulty by 1.

vehicle.name: Kelsail Dust Sled
vehicle.encumbranceCapacity: 100 (without passengers)

abilities.name: All-Terrain
abilities.description: When making a {@skill Driving} check to direct the vehicle, your character may remove {@dice setback|2} added to the check due to terrain.

description: When most visitors to {@rule Kenara System|Kenara's|eoti} three worlds think of dust sleds, they visualize the great sleds pulled by vast herds of Tuuran beasts, carrying whole cities through the deserts in search of cooler climates as the seasons shift. However, the {@rule Emirates of Hacan|Hacan|eoti} have traditionally used dust sleds of all sizes to travel across the dunes of their homeworlds, and many of the smaller models use modern drive units instead of being pulled by draft animals.

The Kelsail is a prototypical example of these latter types, large enough to carry a dozen passengers and held a few meters above the desert by modern contragrav systems. Constructed by the thousand in the orbital factories of the Morghish Emirate, it has been adopted by many of the ordrim as a cargo and troop transporter due to its cheapness, reliability, and customization options. The Kelsail has a stubby body with a rounded nose and short wings. It comes open-topped as standard, but crew bubbles and enclosed passenger compartments are some of the more common modifications. Likewise, the passenger space can be easily converted for cargo hauling in a matter of minutes.

The Kelsail is not armed as standard, but some of the ordrim use variants as scouting vehicles and give them an array of light weapons. The Lances of the Sand Seas from Alkahis Emirate are particularly known for using armed Kelsails to support their patrol and policing efforts. They prefer these dust sleds to purpose-built military vehicles because their engines are almost entirely silent and they leave no tracks in the sand.

vehicle.name: Kelsail Dust Sled (Armed)
vehicle.encumbranceCapacity: 100 (without passengers)

abilities.name: All-Terrain
abilities.description: When making a {@skill Driving} check to direct the vehicle, your character may remove {@dice setback|2} added to the check due to terrain.
